title: Vectors
summary: Vec<T>, the growable list: creating, pushing, reading with [] and get, why a reference blocks push, iterating, storing several types with an enum, and how a Vec grows.

blocks.md: Arrays and tuples have a fixed size known at compile time. The standard library's **collections** hold any number of values, stored on the heap, so they can grow and shrink while the program runs. The most used of all is **`Vec<T>`**, a *vector*: a list of values of one type `T`, stored next to each other in memory.

blocks.explain: `push` adds to the end, so the vector must be `mut`. When a vector is dropped, all its elements are dropped with it.

blocks.title: Reading elements
blocks.md:
There are two ways to read an element, and they differ in what happens when the index is past the end:

- `&v[i]` gives a reference to the element, and **panics** if there is none. Use it when a bad index is a bug.
- `v.get(i)` gives an `Option<&T>`: `Some(&element)` or `None`. Use it when an index might legitimately be out of range, such as a number typed by a user.

blocks.explain: Why should a reference to the **first** element care about a push at the **end**? Because a vector stores its elements side by side. If there is no room for one more, `push` allocates a bigger block, copies the elements there and frees the old block, and `first` would point at freed memory. The borrowing rules from chapter 4 prevent exactly that.

blocks.title: Iterating
blocks.md: `for` over `&v` borrows each element; over `&mut v` lets you change each one (with `*`); over `v` itself moves the elements out and consumes the vector.

blocks.explain: `v.iter()` gives an iterator over references, which methods like `sum` and `max` consume. Chapter 13 covers iterators; you will use them constantly.

blocks.md: A vector holds one type. When you need a list of different kinds of things, such as the cells of a spreadsheet row, define an enum whose variants hold the different types. The vector then holds the enum, and `match` makes you handle every kind:

blocks.title: Capacity
blocks.md: A vector keeps three values on the stack: a pointer to its heap buffer, its **length** (elements in use) and its **capacity** (elements the buffer can hold). When length reaches capacity, `push` allocates a buffer about twice as big. If you know how many elements are coming, `Vec::with_capacity(n)` allocates once up front.

blocks.title: Grades
blocks.md: `grades` holds test scores. Print the number of scores, the average with one decimal, the highest score, and the scores sorted from high to low. `sort()` sorts low to high, and `reverse()` reverses a vector in place.
blocks.task: Print `5 scores, average 78.4, best 95` and then `[95, 88, 76, 70, 63]`.
hints: `let total: i32 = grades.iter().sum();` then divide as `f64`: `total as f64 / grades.len() as f64`.
`grades.iter().max()` is an `Option<&i32>`; `.unwrap()` is fine here because the list is not empty.
Print the first line **before** sorting, or use `best` from before: `max` borrows `grades`, so finish using `best` before calling `sort`.

blocks.title: Working with lists
blocks.goal: Write vector functions that cover reading, building new vectors, and changing them in place.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn evens(values: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>`: a new vector with only the even numbers, in order.
- `pub fn running_total(values: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>`: each element is the sum of all values up to and including that position.
- `pub fn remove_duplicates(values: &mut Vec<i32>)`: keep the first occurrence of each value, in the original order.
- `pub fn median(values: &[f64]) -> Option<f64>`: the middle value after sorting (the mean of the two middle values for an even count); `None` for an empty slice.
hints: Build results with `let mut out = Vec::new();` and `out.push(...)`.
`remove_duplicates`: build a new `Vec` of values you have seen (`if !seen.contains(&v) { seen.push(v) }`), then `*values = seen;`.
`median`: copy into a new vector with `values.to_vec()`, then sort floats with `sorted.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap())` (floats have no total order because of NaN).
blocks.solution_explain: `with_capacity` avoids regrowing because the final length is known. `remove_duplicates` is quadratic because `contains` scans the list; with a `HashSet` (lesson 3) it would be linear. `median` copies the data so the caller's order is untouched.

points: `Vec<T>` is a growable list on the heap: `Vec::new()`, `vec![...]`, `push`, `pop`.
`&v[i]` panics past the end; `v.get(i)` returns an `Option`.
Holding a reference into a vector blocks changes that might reallocate it.
An enum lets one vector hold several kinds of values.
Length versus capacity: `with_capacity` allocates once when you know the size.
